text:
A: Hiya mate, can you hear me?
B: Loud and clear. Colin, Worthing. You must be the barm man.
A: Ha! Has Lorraine been talking about me?
B: She has. She thinks barm's daft. I said I'd not tell you, so I've told you straight away.
A: She was dead set on bap. I respect it. I'm Craig, Lancaster. Your photo, honestly, you look like my dad. That's a good thing.
B: I'll take it. I see you've got a bike in the front room. Maureen'd have that out the door.
A: Nadia's given up. I run a bike shop, so it's sort of an occupational hazard. I do up old bikes on the side as well, sell them on or give them to the lads at the youth club round the corner.
B: Oh, do you now. That's interesting, that. I've been meaning, for about two years, mind, to do some woodwork teaching. Men's shed or a youth project. I was a joiner, see, forty-odd years. Took a couple of apprentices on, and honestly that was the best bit of the whole job, showing a young lad how to cut a joint properly and seeing him get it. One of them still sends me a Christmas card. He had a rough patch with the drink a while back and I kept an eye on him, and he's doing alright now. So I sort of think, I've got all this in my hands and it's sitting in a shed.
A: You should, mate. Seriously. Teaching a kid to fix a puncture, they're made up for a week.
B: Same principle, isn't it. Your hands do something and it works.
A: That's the dream for me, actually. Long-term I want a little workshop-café. Fix bikes in the back, coffee in the front, maybe a bench where people can learn to do their own.
B: Now that I'd come to. Would you have a cake?
A: Obviously. Non-negotiable. Do you still do woodwork, then?
B: Turning, mostly. Bowls. I've got one on now out of old cherry, it's gone a bit lopsided.
A: Character.
B: That's what I said! Where do you go on holiday, then, you look like you get about.
A: Pyrenees on the bike, Lisbon last year. I really want to do Japan before I'm forty.
B: Japan! Me too. Before the knees go. It's the temples I want to see, the old wooden ones, they're put together without a nail, some of them. Joints you wouldn't believe.
A: No nails, really?
B: Hardly any. Hundreds of years standing. I'd just stand there with my mouth open.
A: We should go together, honestly. I'll plan it, you can explain the beams.
B: Deal. Is your dad a joiner, then, if I look like him?
A: Forklift, at the truck plant in Leyland. He's not been brilliant lately, health-wise. I'm trying to get over more.
B: You do that. My dad went at fifty-eight. You don't think you'll miss the ordinary stuff, but you —
